read.sections.0.heading.source: Mistakes can come from missing examples
read.sections.0.heading.back: Mistakes can come from missing examples

read.sections.0.text.source: In Lesson 3, the leaf model made mistakes when its training data left something out. Real AI tools can go wrong in the same way. At Riverbend Learning Centre, a voice typing tool worked well for the adult teachers, but it typed many words wrongly for the youngest learners. The tool had learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were new to it. Researchers have found this problem in real life too. Many speech tools are much less accurate with children's voices. One reason is that there are far fewer recordings of children for the tools to learn from.
read.sections.0.text.back: In Lesson 3, the leaf model made mistakes when its training data did not include something. Real AI tools can go wrong in the same way. At Riverbend Learning Centre, a voice typing tool worked well for the adult teachers, but the tool typed many words wrongly for the youngest learners. The tool learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were still new to it. Researchers have also found this problem in real life. Many speech tools are much less accurate for children's voices. One reason is that there are far fewer recordings of children that those tools can learn from.

read.sections.1.heading.source: When a group is left out, AI can be unfair
read.sections.1.heading.back: When a group is left out, AI can be unfair

read.sections.1.text.source: When a tool works well for some groups of people and badly for others, we say that it has a bias. Missing examples are one possible cause. Others are wrong or unfair labels, a goal that suits some people more than others, a design choice, or using a tool in a place it wasn't made for. The Riverbend translation tool makes many more mistakes in languages with little writing online. Researchers have found the same pattern in real AI language tools. Even when nobody meant to leave people out, the result can still be unfair.
read.sections.1.text.back: When a tool works well for some groups of people and badly for other groups, we say the tool has a bias. Missing examples are one possible cause. Other causes are wrong or unfair labels, a goal that suits some people more than others, a choice in its design, or using a tool in a place it was not made for. The translation tool at Riverbend makes many more mistakes in languages that have only a little writing on the internet. Researchers found the same pattern in real AI language tools. Even when nobody meant to leave other people out, the result can still be unfair.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some tools work well for some people and badly for others. This is called bias. Missing examples are one cause. Wrong labels are another. So is a goal or design that suits some people more. Using a tool in the wrong place can cause it too. The Riverbend translation tool makes more mistakes in some languages. They have little writing online. Researchers found this with real tools too. Even if nobody meant to leave people out, it can be unfair.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Some tools work well for some people and badly for other people. This is called bias. Missing examples are one of its causes. Wrong labels are another cause. So is a goal or design that suits some people more. Using a tool in the wrong place can also be its cause. The translation tool at Riverbend makes more mistakes in some languages. Those languages have only a little writing on the internet. Researchers also found this in real tools. Even if nobody meant to leave other people out, the result can be unfair.

read.sections.2.text.source: To find bias, people test a tool with many different groups, not only with the people who built it. Then they compare the results. A gap in the results shows that something is wrong, but not why. So they look for the cause. Are some people's examples missing? Are the labels wrong? Was the tool made for a different goal or place? If examples are missing, they can collect more, but only with people's permission. More data does not fix every cause. If the labels are unfair, more examples with the same labels won't help. For important decisions, a person should always check what the AI says.
read.sections.2.text.back: To find bias, people test a tool with many different groups, not only with the people who made it. Then they compare the results. A gap in the results shows that something is wrong, but does not show why. So they look for the cause. Are some people's examples missing? Are the labels wrong? Was the tool made for another goal or place? If examples are missing, they can collect more, but only with the permission of the people. More data does not fix every cause. If the labels are unfair, more examples with the same labels will not help. For important decisions, a person must always check what the AI says.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: To find bias, test the tool with many groups and compare the results. A gap shows that something is wrong, but not why. So look for the cause. Are examples missing? Are labels wrong? Was the tool made for another goal or place? Missing examples can be added, if people agree. But more data does not fix everything. Unfair labels stay unfair. For big decisions, a person should check the AI.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: To find bias, test that tool with many groups and compare the results. A gap shows something is wrong, but does not show why. So look for the cause. Are any examples missing? Are the labels wrong? Was the tool made for another goal or place? Missing examples can be added, if the people agree. But more data does not fix everything. Unfair labels stay unfair. For big decisions, a person must check that AI.

watch.afterQuestion.source: What two questions should you ask about any training data?
watch.afterQuestion.back: What two questions should you ask about any training data?

watch.summary.source: This video explains why training data matters so much. A machine learning tool is only as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video site keeps track of what people watch, sometimes without them knowing. Then it uses that data to suggest more videos. In health care, experts label thousands of medical pictures, so a computer can learn to spot illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most of the X-ray pictures come from men. Then the tool may make more mistakes for women. People can put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data. Is there enough of it? Does it include many kinds of people and situations?
watch.summary.back: This video explains why training data is so important. A machine learning tool is only as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video site records what people watch, sometimes without them knowing. Then that site uses that data to suggest more videos. In health care, experts label thousands of medical pictures, so that a computer can learn to recognise illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most of the X-ray pictures come from men. Then the tool may make more mistakes for women. People can put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data. Is there enough data? Does that data include many kinds of people and situations?

educatorNotes.0.source: The numbers in the activity (19, 16 and 9 of 20) are made up to show the idea; the Riverbend table tells learners what each tool learned from, so the cause is given, not worked out from the scores. Real research: Kid-Whisper (AIES 2024) found that a widely used speech tool, without extra training, made 3 to 10 times as many errors on children's speech as on adults' in the tests it used, and names two causes: few recordings of children, and children's speech varying more as they grow. Training it on more children's speech narrowed the gap but did not close it.

Real research: Kid-Whisper (AIES 2024) found that a widely used speech tool, without extra training, made 3 to 10 times more mistakes on children's speech than on adults' speech in the tests it used, and names two causes: the small number of recordings of children, and children's speech varying more as they grow. Training it with more children's speech narrowed the gap, but did not close it.

educatorNotes.1.source: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag (2021) list seven sources of harm across the machine-learning life cycle, including who is in the data (representation), how labels are chosen or measured, the goal a model is trained for, how it is tested, and how and where it is used. Their example: a heart-attack model improved when more data from women was added, but a hiring model trained on human ratings did not, because the problem was in the labels. A gap in results shows something is wrong, not why. Don't tell learners that bias is always an accident: the lesson says only that it can be unfair even when nobody meant it. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md. Lesson 3's leaf model is reused on purpose: learners can see one cause (missing examples) in a small model they trained and in real tools. The activity's extension (a wrong label copied by the model) shows a second cause, labels.
educatorNotes.1.back: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag (2021) name seven sources of harm along the machine-learning life cycle, including who is in the data (representation), how labels are chosen or measured, the goal a model is trained for, how a model is tested, and how and where a model is used. Their example: a heart-attack model became better when more data from women was added, but a hiring model trained on human ratings did not become better, because the problem was in the labels. A gap in results shows that something is wrong, not why. Don't tell learners that bias always happens by accident: this lesson only says that the result can be unfair even when nobody meant it. Its claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md. Lesson 3's leaf model is used again on purpose: learners can see one cause (missing examples) in a small model they trained themselves and in real tools. This activity's extension (a wrong label copied by the model) shows a second cause, labels.
